title: D-Day: The Normandy Landings, 6 June 1944
summary: Hour by hour through the largest seaborne invasion in history: paratroopers in the night, the bombardment, the five beaches and the first German counter-attack.

sides.name: German
sides.description: Nazi Germany's 7th Army, occupying France since 1940

arrows.label: USS Texas fires on Pointe du Hoc
USS Arkansas fires on the Omaha bluffs
HMS Ajax fires on the Longues battery
German battery fires on the Utah fleet

events.title: Pegasus Bridge captured
events.text: Glider troops land metres from the bridge over the Caen canal and take it in about ten minutes.

events.title: Paratroopers scattered
events.text: Cloud and anti-aircraft fire scatter US paratroopers far from their drop zones. Small groups fight wherever they land.

events.title: Sainte-Mère-Église liberated
events.text: The first town in France liberated by the Allies.

events.title: Naval bombardment begins
events.text: Seven battleships, more than 20 cruisers and over 100 destroyers open fire on the German defences.

events.title: H-Hour: Utah Beach
events.text: Currents push the landing craft 2 km south of the target, onto a weakly defended stretch. Losses are light.

events.title: H-Hour: Omaha Beach
events.text: Bombs have missed the bluffs. Machine-gun fire pins the first waves on the beach.

events.title: Rangers climb Pointe du Hoc
events.text: The 2nd Rangers scale 30 m cliffs with ropes and ladders and find the big guns have been moved inland. They track them down and destroy them.

events.title: Gold and Sword landings
events.text: British troops land with specialised tanks that clear mines and cross obstacles.

events.title: Juno Beach landing
events.text: Rough seas delay the Canadians. They take heavy losses at the sea wall but push furthest inland of any force that day.

events.title: Omaha exit opened
events.text: Small groups led by junior officers and sergeants climb the bluffs. The Vierville exit is cleared.

events.title: German tanks counter-attack
events.text: The 21st Panzer Division makes the only major German armoured counter-attack of the day.

events.title: German tanks reach the coast
events.text: A German battle group slips through the gap between Juno and Sword to the sea, then pulls back.

events.title: End of D-Day
events.text: About 156,000 Allied troops are ashore. About 4,400 have been killed. German losses are estimated at 4,000–9,000.

story.title: Fortress Europe
story.text:
By 1944 Nazi Germany had occupied France for four years and fortified the coast with bunkers, mines and beach obstacles: the **Atlantic Wall**. The Allies (the **United States**, **Britain**, **Canada** and others) planned **Operation Overlord**, an invasion across the English Channel to open a second front against Germany.

Deception plans convinced German commanders that the main attack would come at **Calais**, far to the east. Bad weather almost cancelled everything. General **Eisenhower** gave the order to go on 6 June.

question.prompt: Why did the Allies work so hard to make Germany expect an attack at Calais?
choices: So German reserves would be kept away from Normandy
Because Calais had no defences at all
To give the French Resistance time to leave Calais
question.explain: Calais is the shortest crossing, so it was believable. Every German division held back to guard it was one fewer division to counter-attack in Normandy.

story.title: Paratroopers in the dark
story.text:
Shortly after midnight about **13,000 American** and almost **8,000 British** paratroopers and glider troops landed behind the beaches. Their job was to seize bridges and road exits and block German reinforcements.

British gliders captured **Pegasus Bridge** in minutes. The Americans were badly **scattered** by cloud and flak, but small groups fought wherever they landed. Their confusion also confused the Germans.

story.title: The armada and the bombardment
story.text:
Nearly **7,000 vessels** crossed the Channel overnight: warships, transports and thousands of landing craft. At dawn battleships and cruisers began a huge **naval bombardment**, while bombers attacked the beach defences.

Many bombs fell too far inland, especially at Omaha, because the crews feared hitting their own landing craft.

story.title: Utah and Pointe du Hoc
story.text:
At **6:30** American troops landed at **Utah Beach**. The current carried them south of the target, to a lightly defended stretch, and they lost fewer than 200 men.

To the east, the **2nd Rangers** climbed the cliffs of **Pointe du Hoc** under fire to silence guns that threatened both American beaches.

question.prompt: Click on the map where the Americans landed with the fewest losses.
question.explain: Utah Beach, on the east coast of the Cotentin peninsula. Landing in the 'wrong' place turned out to be lucky.

story.title: Bloody Omaha
story.text:
**Omaha Beach** was the hardest. High bluffs overlooked the beach, the bombing had missed, and many amphibious tanks sank in rough water. The first waves were pinned down on the sand and suffered terrible casualties.

By late morning, small groups led by sergeants and junior officers worked their way up the bluffs, and the **Vierville exit** was opened. By night the Americans held a narrow strip about 2 km deep, at the cost of around **2,400** casualties.

question.prompt: What was the main reason Omaha Beach was so much deadlier than Utah?
choices: Defenders on high bluffs, with the bombing having missed them
The Americans landed there at night
The beach was defended by tanks and nothing else
question.explain: The terrain favoured the defenders, and the preparation that should have weakened them (bombs, amphibious tanks) largely failed.

story.title: Gold, Juno and Sword
story.text:
British troops landed at **Gold** and **Sword**, and the Canadians at **Juno**. Specialised tanks ("Hobart's Funnies") cleared mines and bridged ditches.

The Canadians suffered about 1,000 casualties at Juno, yet pushed further inland than anyone else that day. Commandos marched from Sword to link up with the paratroopers at Pegasus Bridge.

story.title: The German response
story.text:
German defenders fought hard, but their high command was slow. **Rommel** was in Germany for his wife's birthday, and the powerful tank reserves could only move with **Hitler's** permission.

The **21st Panzer Division** counter-attacked in the afternoon and some tanks reached the sea between Juno and Sword, but they pulled back for fear of being cut off.

question.prompt: Why didn't German tank divisions crush the landings on 6 June?
choices: Confusion, absent commanders and orders that had to come from Hitler
Germany had no tanks in France
The tanks were all waiting at Pointe du Hoc
question.explain: There were several panzer divisions in France, but the Calais deception, Rommel's absence and Hitler's control of the reserves delayed them on the critical day.

story.title: After D-Day
story.text:
By midnight about **156,000** Allied troops were ashore. The cost was about **4,400** Allied dead, and thousands of German soldiers and French civilians also died that day. Many Normans lost their homes in the bombing that followed.

The beaches were not yet joined up, and it took nearly three months of hard fighting before **Paris was liberated** on 25 August 1944. But the second front was open, and Germany now faced enemies on three sides.

Stephen E. Ambrose, D-Day, June 6, 1944: The Climactic Battle of World War II (1994)
The D-Day Story museum, Portsmouth: theddaystory.com
